cells.tense: You are here with the pen, and the writing is going well today.
cells.act: build the smallest structure that holds it
cells.ask: Take something you're deciding right now. Put it on one page — the pieces in the order they have to happen, the fewest moving parts. Finish the page today, then choose from inside it.
cells.core:
You read a situation before you can say how you read it, and what you notice holds up. Here, where you pick a direction, a hunch can sit unproven for a while and you'll still move on it. Nothing has to be argued first. Your reading shows itself in the act of deciding, not ahead of it, and that ease is the point — you aren't waiting for certainty to arrive before you move.

Give the next real decision somewhere to live. Put the pieces on one page, in the order they have to happen, so you can walk away and come back without rebuilding the whole picture in your head. A container like that serves what it carries. When there's more on your plate than you can hold at once, it's what keeps the plain sense of things in view instead of buried under noise. Then decide from inside it.

cells.verb: knowing what to attend to, before you can say why
cells.place: where you choose a direction and mean it

cells.tense: You are braced at a future you cannot write in, gathering more than the decision needs.
cells.act: move toward the thing you actually want
cells.ask: Stop gathering and say to yourself what you want out of this, then take one small step toward that — a call, a reply, a yes. No clock on it; do it when you notice the pile growing.
cells.core:
When the road ahead can't be written in, taking in more starts to feel like the way through. You collect everything you might need and hold off deciding, and the pile grows past what the choice asks for. Noticing turns into standing still — every angle gets covered twice while the appetite underneath goes unconsulted.

A decision leans in a direction, and direction comes from wanting something, not from covering every angle. Name what you want out of this, plainly, where only you can hear it. Then move one small step toward it. The step matters less than facing what you want. More gathering won't decide this. You decide it, and you can do that with less than you're holding.
cells.sheetLine: You're gathering past the point where it helps.
cells.verb: knowing what to attend to, before you can say why
cells.place: where you choose a direction and mean it

cells.tense: You are at a door that is already behind you, waiting for someone to confirm what you saw.
cells.act: take the next step with only enough light for that step
cells.ask: Pick the thing you keep asking others about, and take its next step from your own sense. No second opinion first. No deadline — just the next step, when you're ready.
cells.core:
What you see keeps getting checked against other people. You ask someone what they think of a thing, and their answer becomes what decides it. Nothing in you is aimed anywhere while the verdict is out. Your reading sits there and gets treated as if it were only a guess, and the standing-still is the whole shape of it.

Nobody is handed the whole road before they walk it. Enough light for one step is what anyone gets. Take the next step in the thing you've been outsourcing, and use what you already see. If you're wrong, the world will correct you and you'll keep your footing — the waiting is what has been running while the errors never came. Your own eyes are enough for one small move.
cells.sheetLine: You keep asking others what you saw yourself.
cells.verb: knowing what to attend to, before you can say why

cells.tense: You are present, pen down, and writing anyway inside a room you don't remember entering.
cells.act: give back what is owed, and take what is yours
cells.ask: When a read lands and you can't place where it came from, jot one line about it that day. Keep it up for a week or two. Then read the lines back and put your own name on them.
cells.core:
Your reading of a room runs ahead of your account of it. Something gets noticed, the choice bends toward it, and afterward it looks like luck or a mood passing through. The decisions keep landing well, and you keep filing them under random. What's steering is yours, and it's the last thing you'd credit.

Keep the record straight for a while. When a read arrives and its source won't show, write one line that day, no more. Later, look back at those lines and recognize them as your work — a clear eye doesn't need an entrance to count. Nothing grand is owed anyone here. You're only putting your own name on what you already used, and the surprise fades once it's in your hand.
cells.sheetLine: You call the decisions random. You're making them.
cells.verb: knowing what to attend to, before you can say why
cells.place: where you choose a direction and mean it

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person's decisions have actually proved accurate — the record supports perceptions landing without argument, not outcomes, so every cell leans on the knowing itself and never on results. A reader could reasonably say the confusion is plain exhaustion or too many people's opinions in the room, not a lost capacity; the asks still stand if that's true, since each one is done small and the person can say it isn't what's happening and keep the act anyway. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'perceptions land without argument' — it sounds like a verdict on their mind, so I've kept it out of the glass entirely and let the reading stay about whether they move on what they notice.
